newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Honduras military could act against protests.
newsitem.headline: Honduras military could act against protests.

text.p: Honduras' Minister of Defence, Col. Jose Nunez, on Sunday said the military could take action to calm the Central American nation, which faces another week of labour unrest.
"The armed forces will carry out the orders of the courts. We have to follow the law," Nunez said.
On Friday tens of thousands of government workers launched a strike to demand higher wages, seizing control of several government buildings and bringing most official activity to a halt.
Up to 23,000 workers took part in the strike, demanding a freezing of prices, lower transportation costs, as well as better pay.
The National Association of Honduran Public Employess (ANDEPH) said on Sunday that it will temporarily suspend its strkes to allow negotiations to take place.
But public health sector workers said they would start escalating strikes starting on Monday, with the aim of eventually paralysing hospitals and health centres to back their demands.
On Saturday an important business leader said the country was facing a crisis similar to that in Ecuador, where President Abdala Bucaram was forced out of power.
"In Honduras we could see a crisis like that seen in Ecuador. We have the same conditions," the president of the National Association of Business Leaders, Adolfo Facusse, said.
This is the first major public workers' strike faced by the government of President Carlos Roberto Reina, who took power in 1994 and leaves this year after general elections.
Honduras is one of Latin America's poorest countries.

The strike comes following a government move to raise spending on public workers' salaries by $21.6 million (276 million lempiras) -- an increase that fell short of their demands for an increase of $70.5 million (900 million lempiras) on public salaries.
